arXiv:2503.24076v2 [math.CO] 14 Oct 2026

On a question about real-rooted polynomials and ff-polynomials of simplicial complexes

Lili Mu Address: School of Mathematics and Statistics, Jiangsu Normal University, Xuzhou 221116, PR China Email address: lilimu@jsnu.edu.cn and Volkmar Welker Address: Philipps-Universität Marburg, Fachbereich Mathematik und Informatik, 35032 Marburg, Germany Email address: welker@mathematik.uni-marburg.de
Abstract.

For a polynomial f⁡(t)=1+f0​t+⋯+fd−1​tdf(t)=1+f_{0}t+\cdots+f_{d-1}t^{d} with positive integer coefficients Bell and Skandera [Discrete Math, 307 (2007), pp. 668-682] ask if real-rootedness of f⁡(t)f(t) implies that there is a simplicial complex with ff-vector (1,f0,…,fd−1)(1,f_{0},\ldots,f_{d-1}) or equivalently a simplicial complex with ff-polynomial f⁡(t)f(t). In this paper we discover properties implied by the real-rootedness of f⁡(t)f(t) in terms of the binomial representation fi=(xi+1i+1)f_{i}=\binom{x_{i+1}}{i+1}, i≥0i\geq 0. We use these to partially answer the question by Bell and Skandera. We also describe two further approaches to the question and use one to verify that some well studied real-rooted classical polynomials are ff-polynomials.

Finally, we provide a series of results showing that the set of ff-vectors of simplicial complexes is closed under constructions also preserving real-rootedness of their generating polynomials.

1. Introduction

The results of this paper are motivated by a question of Bell and Skandera.

Question 1.0 (Bell and Skandera, Question 1.1 in [2]).

Let f⁡(t)=1+f0​t+⋯+fd−1​tdf(t)=1+f_{0}t+\cdots+f_{d-1}t^{d} be a polynomial with positive integer coefficients. If f⁡(t)f(t) is real-rooted, is (1,f0,…,fd−1)(1,f_{0},\ldots,f_{d-1}) the ff-vector (f−1Δ,…,fd−1Δ)(f_{-1}^{\Delta},\ldots,f_{d-1}^{\Delta}) of a simplicial complex Δ\Delta?

Recall that for a simplicial complex Δ\Delta the entries fiΔf_{i}^{\Delta} of the ff-vector are the number of ii-dimensional faces of Δ\Delta. Thus in other words the conclusion of Question 1.0 is that f​(t)=fΔ​(t)f(t)=f^{\Delta}(t) is the ff-polynomial of a simplicial complex Δ\Delta. We develop three approaches to this question, which may be of independent interest, and collect further evidence for a positive answer to the question. The main results of the paper are.

  • •

    For a real-rooted polynomial f⁡(t)=1+f0​t+⋯+fd−1​tdf(t)=1+f_{0}t+\cdots+f_{d-1}t^{d} with positive integer coefficients and real numbers xi≥ix_{i}\geq i such that f⁡(t)=1+(x11)​t+⋯+(xdd)​tdf(t)=1+\binom{x_{1}}{1}t+\cdots+\binom{x_{d}}{d}t^{d} we have x1≥⋯≥xdx_{1}\geq\cdots\geq x_{d} (Theorem 3.0). As a consequence we provide in Corollary 3.0 a new proof of [2, Theorem 4.2] showing that real-rootedness of f⁡(t)f(t) implies that the coefficient sequence is the ff-vector of a multicomplex or equivalently the hh-vector of a Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complex.

  • •

    If f⁡(t)=1+(x11)​t+⋯+(xdd)​tdf(t)=1+\binom{x_{1}}{1}t+\cdots+\binom{x_{d}}{d}t^{d} is a real-rooted polynomial with positive integer coefficients, and xi≥⌈xi+1⌉x_{i}\geq\lceil x_{i+1}\rceil then there is a simplicial complex Δ\Delta such that f⁡(t)f(t) is the ff-polynomial of Δ\Delta (Theorem 3.0).

  • •

    A method based on Murai’s [16] admissible vectors which can be used to demonstrate that classical real-rooted polynomials (Eulerian, Stirling, derangement) are ff-polynomials of simplicial complexes. For Eulerian polynomials this is a known result (see [10, 7]).

  • •

    Proofs that classical constructions preserving real-rootedness applied to ff-polynomials fΔ​(t)f^{\Delta}(t) of simplicial complexes yield the ff-polynomial of another simplicial complex (see Section 4).

2. Notation, definitions and basic results

For a finite set Ω\Omega, a simplicial complex over ground set Ω\Omega is a set of subsets of Ω\Omega such that σ⊆τ∈Δ\sigma\subseteq\tau\in\Delta implies σ∈Δ\sigma\in\Delta. We call a σ∈Δ\sigma\in\Delta a face of Δ\Delta and the dimension of a face σ\sigma is dim(σ)=#​σ−1\dim(\sigma)=\#\sigma-1. The dimension of Δ\Delta is max⁡dimσ∈Δ⁡(σ)\max_{\sigma\in\Delta}\dim(\sigma). If Δ\Delta is a dd-dimensional simplicial complex then the vector fΔ=(f−1Δ,…,fdΔ)f^{\Delta}=(f_{-1}^{\Delta},\ldots,f_{d}^{\Delta}) where fiΔ=#⁡{σ∈Δ|dim(σ)=i}f_{i}^{\Delta}=\#\big\{\,\sigma\in\Delta~\big|~\dim(\sigma)=i\,\big\} is called the ff-vector of Δ\Delta and fΔ​(t)=f−1Δ+f0Δ​t+⋯+fdΔ​td+1f^{\Delta}(t)=f_{-1}^{\Delta}+f_{0}^{\Delta}t+\cdots+f_{d}^{\Delta}t^{d+1} is called the ff-polynomial of Δ\Delta. Expanding (1−t)d⋅fΔ​(11−t)=hΔ​(t)=h0Δ+h1Δ​t+⋯+hd+1Δ​td+1(1-t)^{d}\cdot f^{\Delta}\big(\,\frac{1}{1-t}\,\big)=h^{\Delta}(t)=h_{0}^{\Delta}+h_{1}^{\Delta}t+\cdots+h_{d+1}^{\Delta}t^{d+1} yields the hh-polynomial with coefficient sequence hΔ=(h0Δ,…,hd+1Δ)h^{\Delta}=(h_{0}^{\Delta},\ldots,h_{d+1}^{\Delta}) the hh-vector of Δ\Delta. For a face F∈ΔF\in\Delta, denote by lkΔ(F)={G:F∪G∈Δ,F∩G=∅}\mathrm{lk}_{\Delta}(F)=\big\{\,G\,:\,F\cup G\in\Delta,F\cap G=\emptyset\,\big\} the link of FF in Δ\Delta.

It is well-known that the ff-vector of a simplicial complex can be characterized in terms of functions based upon the following expression of a positive integer mm as a sum of binomial coefficients. Given a positive integer ii, there exists a unique representation of mm in the form

m=(aii)+(ai−1i−1)+⋯+(ajj),m=\binom{a_{i}}{i}+\binom{a_{i-1}}{i-1}+\cdots+\binom{a_{j}}{j},

where ai>ai−1>⋯>aj≥j≥1a_{i}>a_{i-1}>\cdots>a_{j}\geq j\geq 1. We refer to this representation of mm as the iith binomial expansion of mm. Since the binomial representation of mm is unique it follows that

(1) m=(aii)+(ai−1i−1)+⋯+(ajj)\displaystyle m=\binom{a_{i}}{i}+\binom{a_{i-1}}{i-1}+\cdots+\binom{a_{j}}{j} <(ai+1i).\displaystyle<\binom{a_{i}+1}{i}.

Define the functions (μi)i≥1(\mu_{i})_{i\geq 1} and (κi)i≥1(\kappa_{i})_{i\geq 1} on ℕ\mathbb{N} by

μi​(m)=(aii−1)+(ai−1i−2)+⋯+(ajj−1)\mu_{i}(m)=\binom{a_{i}}{i-1}+\binom{a_{i-1}}{i-2}+\cdots+\binom{a_{j}}{j-1}

and

κi​(m)=(ai−1i−1)+(ai−1−1i−2)+⋯+(aj−1j−1).\kappa_{i}(m)=\binom{a_{i}-1}{i-1}+\binom{a_{i-1}-1}{i-2}+\cdots+\binom{a_{j}-1}{j-1}.

The characterization of ff- and hh-vectors of simplicial complexes are due to Kruskal [13], Katona [12] independently and Macaulay [15] respectively. Note that in combinatorial terms Macaulay’s result characterizes ff-vectors of multicomplexes which is equivalent to being the hh-vector of a Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complex, see e.g. [18] for the equivalence and the definition of Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complexes.

Theorem 2.0 (Kruskal-Katona, Macaulay).

Let f=(1,f0,…,fd−1)f=(1,f_{0},\dots,f_{d-1}) be a vector of positive integers. Then

  • •

    ff is an ff-vector of a simplicial complex if and only if μi+1​(fi)≤fi−1\mu_{i+1}(f_{i})\leq f_{i-1} for 0≤i≤d−10\leq i\leq d-1.

  • •

    ff is an hh-vector of a Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complex if and only if κi+1​(fi)≤fi−1\kappa_{i+1}(f_{i})\leq f_{i-1} for 0≤i≤d−10\leq i\leq d-1.

As usual, for example in the contexts of Newton’s generalized binomial formula, we consider the binomial coefficient (nk)\binom{n}{k} as a polynomial function in nn, so that for x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} we have

(xk)=x(x−1)⋯(x−k+1)k!.\binom{x}{k}=\frac{x(x-1)\cdots(x-k+1)}{k!}.

We also write (x)k(x)_{k} for the numerator x(x−1)⋯(x−k+1)x(x-1)\cdots(x-k+1). The following lemma recalls some well known facts about binomial coefficients.

Lemma 2.1.
  • (i)

    For any x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} and any 0<k∈ℕ0<k\in\mathbb{N} we have (xk)+(xk−1)=(x+1k)\binom{x}{k}+\binom{x}{k-1}=\binom{x+1}{k}.

  • (ii)

    For any 0≤y∈ℝ0\leq y\in\mathbb{R} and any 0<k∈ℕ0<k\in\mathbb{N} there is a unique x≥k−1x\geq k-1 such that y=(xk)y=\binom{x}{k}.

Proof.

Part (i) is a trivial calculation. The second assertion follows from the fact that k−1k-1 is the largest root of the kk real roots of (xk)\binom{x}{k}. Hence (xk)\binom{x}{k} is strictly monotone for x≥k−1x\geq k-1 with limit +∞+\infty. ∎

By Lemma 2.1 any polynomial f⁡(t)=1+y1​t+⋯+yd​tdf(t)=1+y_{1}t+\cdots+y_{d}t^{d} with coefficients yi≥0y_{i}\geq 0 there are uniquely defined real numbers xi≥i−1x_{i}\geq i-1 such that such that f⁡(t)=1+(x11)​t+⋯+(xdd)​tdf(t)=1+\binom{x_{1}}{1}t+\cdots+\binom{x_{d}}{d}t^{d}. We call (x1,…,xd)(x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}) the binomial expansion of f⁡(t)f(t) or of its coefficient sequence.

3. Real-rooted polynomials with positive integer coefficients

While Question 1.0 remains open, we provide three different approaches to advancing our ability to answer it.

3.1. First approach

We answer a special case of Question 1.0 by describing a subset of real-rooted polynomials in ℕ⁡[t]\mathbb{N}[t] which are provably ff-polynomials of simplicial complexes.

Before we can formulate our first main results we recall the following definition. We say that a polynomial a0+a1​t+⋯+ad​tda_{0}+a_{1}t+\cdots+a_{d}t^{d} of degree dd is ultra log-concave if

[ai(di)]2≥ai−1​ai+1(di−1)​(di+1)\Big[\,\frac{a_{i}}{\binom{d}{i}}\,\Big]^{2}\geq\frac{a_{i-1}a_{i+1}}{\binom{d}{i-1}\binom{d}{i+1}}

for 1≤i≤d−11\leq i\leq d-1. This concept is motivated by Newton’s result showing that any real-rooted polynomial with non-negative coefficients has an ultra log-concave coefficient sequence (see for example [3, Lemma 7.1.1]).

Theorem 3.0.

Let f⁡(t)=1+(x11)​t+⋯+(xdd)​tdf(t)=1+\binom{x_{1}}{1}t+\cdots+\binom{x_{d}}{d}t^{d} in ℝ≥0​[t]\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}[t] with xd≥dx_{d}\geq d be an ultra log-concave polynomial. Then x1≥x2≥⋯≥xdx_{1}\geq x_{2}\geq\cdots\geq x_{d}.

Proof.

By ultra log-concavity we have

(2) [(xii)(di)]2≥(xi−1i−1)(di−1)​(xi+1i+1)(di+1)​ for ​2≤i≤d−1\displaystyle\left[\frac{\binom{x_{i}}{i}}{\binom{d}{i}}\right]^{2}\geq\frac{\binom{x_{i-1}}{i-1}}{\binom{d}{i-1}}\frac{\binom{x_{i+1}}{i+1}}{\binom{d}{i+1}}\text{ for }2\leq i\leq d-1

and

(3) [(x11)(d1)]2≥(x22)(d2).\displaystyle\left[\frac{\binom{x_{1}}{1}}{\binom{d}{1}}\right]^{2}\geq\frac{\binom{x_{2}}{2}}{\binom{d}{2}}.

Claim: For integers 1≤i≤d−11\leq i\leq d-1 we have

(xii)(di)i≥(xii)(di)i+1.\sqrt[i]{\frac{\binom{x_{i}}{i}}{\binom{d}{i}}}\geq\sqrt[i+1]{\frac{\binom{x_{i}}{i}}{\binom{d}{i}}}.

We prove the claim be induction on ii. For i=1i=1 the assertion follows immediately from (3). Now let i>1i>1. Using (2) and the induction hypothesis for i−1i-1 we get

[(xii)(di)]2​≥(2)​(xi−1i−1)(di−1)​(xi+1i+1)(di+1)​≥Induction​[(xii)(di)]i−1i​(xi+1i+1)(di+1).\displaystyle\left[\frac{\binom{x_{i}}{i}}{\binom{d}{i}}\right]^{2}\overset{\text{\eqref{NI}}}{\geq}\frac{\binom{x_{i-1}}{i-1}}{\binom{d}{i-1}}\frac{\binom{x_{i+1}}{i+1}}{\binom{d}{i+1}}\overset{\text{Induction}}{\geq}\left[\frac{\binom{x_{i}}{i}}{\binom{d}{i}}\right]^{\frac{i-1}{i}}\frac{\binom{x_{i+1}}{i+1}}{\binom{d}{i+1}}.

Now cancelling (xii)(di)\frac{\binom{x_{i}}{i}}{\binom{d}{i}} in the left and right terms and taking the (i−1)(i-1)st root yields the claim.

The claim immediately implies the following inequalities

(x11)(d1)≥(x22)(d2)≥⋯≥(xii)(di)i≥⋯≥(xdd)d.\frac{\binom{x_{1}}{1}}{\binom{d}{1}}\geq\sqrt{\frac{\binom{x_{2}}{2}}{\binom{d}{2}}}\geq\cdots\geq\sqrt[i]{\frac{\binom{x_{i}}{i}}{\binom{d}{i}}}\geq\cdots\geq\sqrt[d]{\binom{x_{d}}{d}}.

Then

(xii)≥[(xdd)]i/d​(di).\binom{x_{i}}{i}\geq\left[\binom{x_{d}}{d}\right]^{i/d}\binom{d}{i}.

Since xd≥dx_{d}\geq d we have [(xdd)]i/d≥1\left[\binom{x_{d}}{d}\right]^{i/d}\geq 1 and hence (xii)≥(di)\binom{x_{i}}{i}\geq\binom{d}{i} and xi≥dx_{i}\geq d for all ii.

The proof of the theorem is now by induction on ii. For the case i=1i=1, by (3), we have (d−1)​x12≥d​x2​(x2−1)(d-1)x_{1}^{2}\geq dx_{2}(x_{2}-1). Assume x1<x2x_{1}<x_{2} then

(d−1)​x12<(d−1)​x22≤d​x2​(x2−1),(d-1)x_{1}^{2}<(d-1)x_{2}^{2}\leq dx_{2}(x_{2}-1),

which contradicts (3) and x1≥x2x_{1}\geq x_{2} follows.

For the induction step let i≥2i\geq 2 and assume that xi≤xi−1x_{i}\leq x_{i-1}. By (2),

(xi)i2(d)i2≥(xi−1)i−1(d)i−1​(xi+1)i+1(d)i+1.\frac{(x_{i})_{i}^{2}}{(d)_{i}^{2}}\geq\frac{(x_{i-1})_{i-1}}{(d)_{i-1}}\frac{(x_{i+1})_{i+1}}{(d)_{i+1}}.

By the induction hypothesis,

(xi)i2(d)i2≥(xi)i−1(d)i−1​(xi+1)i+1(d)i+1,\frac{(x_{i})_{i}^{2}}{(d)_{i}^{2}}\geq\frac{(x_{i})_{i-1}}{(d)_{i-1}}\frac{(x_{i+1})_{i+1}}{(d)_{i+1}},

which equivalent to

(4) (d−i)⋅(xi)i⋅(xi−i+1)≥(d−i+1)⋅(xi+1)i+1.\displaystyle(d-i)\cdot(x_{i})_{i}\cdot(x_{i}-i+1)\geq(d-i+1)\cdot(x_{i+1})_{i+1}.

Assume that xi<xi+1x_{i}<x_{i+1}, then

(d−i)⋅(xi)i⋅(xi−i+1)<(d−i)⋅(xi+1)i⋅(xi+1−i+1)≤(d−i+1)⋅(xi+1)i+1,(d-i)\cdot(x_{i})_{i}\cdot(x_{i}-i+1)<(d-i)\cdot(x_{i+1})_{i}\cdot(x_{i+1}-i+1)\leq(d-i+1)\cdot(x_{i+1})_{i+1},

where the last inequality follows from d≤xi+1d\leq x_{i+1}. This contradicts (4) and the proof is complete. ∎

By [4, Example 2.3] and classical results by Newton the assumption of Theorem 3.0 is satisfied in the following two cases.

Corollary 3.0.

Let f⁡(t)=1+(x11)​t+⋯+(xdd)​tdf(t)=1+\binom{x_{1}}{1}t+\cdots+\binom{x_{d}}{d}t^{d} in ℝ≥0​[t]\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}[t] such that xd≥dx_{d}\geq d. Then the following holds:

  • (i)

    If f⁡(t)f(t) is real-rooted then x1≥x2≥⋯≥xdx_{1}\geq x_{2}\geq\cdots\geq x_{d}.

  • (ii)

    If the polynomial sd+(x11)​t​sd−1+(x22)​t2​sd−2+⋯+(xdd)​tds^{d}+\binom{x_{1}}{1}\,ts^{d-1}+\binom{x_{2}}{2}\,t^{2}s^{d-2}+\cdots+\binom{x_{d}}{d}\,t^{d} is Lorentzian then x1≥x2≥⋯≥xdx_{1}\geq x_{2}\geq\cdots\geq x_{d}.

An immediate consequence of Theorem 3.0 is the following result which is the main result in [2], where it is formulated in terms of ff-vectors of multicomplexes.

Corollary 3.0.

Let f⁡(t)=1+f0​t+⋯+fd−1​td∈ℕ⁡[t]f(t)=1+f_{0}t+\cdots+f_{d-1}t^{d}\in\mathbb{N}[t] be a polynomial with only real roots and fi=(xi+1i+1)f_{i}=\binom{x_{i+1}}{i+1}. Then f⁡(t)f(t) is the hh-polynomial of a Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complex.

Proof.

Define x1,…,xdx_{1},\dots,x_{d} by writing fi=(xi+1i+1)f_{i}=\binom{x_{i+1}}{i+1} for i=0,…,d−1i=0,\dots,d-1. Now fix an index ii and let the (i+1)(i+1)st binomial expansion of fif_{i} be

(ai+1i+1)+(aii)+⋯(ajj).\binom{a_{i+1}}{i+1}+\binom{a_{i}}{i}+\cdots\binom{a_{j}}{j}.

By Corollary 3.0, we have

(5) ai+1\displaystyle a_{i+1} ≤xi+1≤xi.\displaystyle\leq x_{i+1}\leq x_{i}.

It follows that

κi+1​(fi)=(ai+1−1i)+(ai−1i−1)+⋯+(aj−1j−1)​≤(1)​(ai+1i)​≤(5)​(xii)=fi−1.\kappa_{i+1}(f_{i})=\binom{a_{i+1}-1}{i}+\binom{a_{i}-1}{i-1}+\cdots+\binom{a_{j}-1}{j-1}\overset{\text{\eqref{eq:binomial}}}{\leq}\binom{a_{i+1}}{i}\overset{\text{\eqref{eq:1}}}{\leq}\binom{x_{i}}{i}=f_{i-1}.

By Theorem 2.0, f⁡(t)f(t) is the hh-polynomial of a simplicial complex. ∎

Now we are position to formulate and prove our main result which provides a positive answer to Question 1.0 in a special case.

Theorem 3.0.

Let f⁡(t)=1+f0​t+⋯+fd−1​td∈ℕ⁡[t]f(t)=1+f_{0}t+\cdots+f_{d-1}t^{d}\in\mathbb{N}[t] be a polynomial of degree dd with only real roots and let f⁡(t)=1+(x11)​t+⋯+(xdd)​td∈ℕ⁡[t]f(t)=1+\binom{x_{1}}{1}t+\cdots+\binom{x_{d}}{d}t^{d}\in\mathbb{N}[t] be its binomial expansion. If xi−1≥⌈xi⌉x_{i-1}\geq\lceil x_{i}\rceil for i=2,…,di=2,\dots,d then f⁡(t)f(t) is the ff-polynomial of a simplicial complex.

Proof.

For a fixed ii in {1,…,d}\{1,\ldots,d\}, let

fi−1=(aii)+(ai−1i−1)+⋯+(ajj),f_{i-1}=\binom{a_{i}}{i}+\binom{a_{i-1}}{i-1}+\cdots+\binom{a_{j}}{j},

with ai>⋯>aj≥j≥a_{i}>\cdots>a_{j}\geq j\geq be the iith binomial expansion of fi−1f_{i-1}. By the monotonicity of (xi)\binom{x}{i} it follows that ai≤xi<ai+1a_{i}\leq x_{i}<a_{i}+1. If ai=xia_{i}=x_{i} then we have fi−1=(xii)=(aii)f_{i-1}=\binom{x_{i}}{i}=\binom{a_{i}}{i} and

μi​(fi−1)=(xii−1)=(⌈xi⌉i−1)≤(xi−1i−1)=fi−2.\mu_{i}(f_{i-1})=\binom{x_{i}}{i-1}=\binom{\lceil x_{i}\rceil}{i-1}\leq\binom{x_{i-1}}{i-1}=f_{i-2}.

If ai<xi<ai+1a_{i}<x_{i}<a_{i}+1 then ai+1=⌈xi⌉≤xi−1a_{i}+1=\lceil x_{i}\rceil\leq x_{i-1}. Hence

μi​(fi−1)=(aii−1)+(ai−1i−2)+⋯+(ajj−1)​≤(1)​(ai+1i−1)≤(xi−1i−1)=fi−2.\mu_{i}(f_{i-1})=\binom{a_{i}}{i-1}+\binom{a_{i-1}}{i-2}+\cdots+\binom{a_{j}}{j-1}\overset{\text{\eqref{eq:binomial}}}{\leq}\binom{a_{i}+1}{i-1}\leq\binom{x_{i-1}}{i-1}=f_{i-2}.

By Theorem 2.0, f⁡(t)f(t) is the ff-polynomial of a simplicial complex. ∎

For the Eulerian polynomial, the Stirling polynomial of the second kind, and the derangement polynomial we have computed the binomial expansion for first 200200 polynomials in each series. In each case the data satisfies the assumptions of Theorem 3.0 (see Figure 1 for some initial values in the case of Eulerian polynomials).

Nevertheless, we were not able to verify the assumptions of Theorem 3.0 for any of these sequences. Instead, we were able to cover them in Corollary 3.0 using our third approach to Question 1.0.

Remark 3.0.

Note that the assumptions xi−1≥⌈xi⌉x_{i-1}\geq\lceil x_{i}\rceil for i=2,…,di=2,\dots,d of Theorem 3.0 is not satisfied by every real-rooted polynomial 1+(x11)​t+⋯+(xdd)​td1+\binom{x_{1}}{1}t+\cdots+\binom{x_{d}}{d}t^{d} in ℕ⁡[t]\mathbb{N}[t] . For example, the polynomial f⁡(t)=1+4​t+5​t2+2​t3=(x+1)2​(2​x+1)f(t)=1+4t+5t^{2}+2t^{3}=(x+1)^{2}(2x+1) has only real roots, but when expressed as f⁡(t)=1+(x11)​t+(x22)+(x33)​t3f(t)=1+\binom{x_{1}}{1}t+\binom{x_{2}}{2}+\binom{x_{3}}{3}t^{3} then x1=4x_{1}=4, x2=12(1+41)=3.701562118⋯x_{2}=\frac{1}{2}(1+\sqrt{41})=3.701562118\cdots and x3=13162+3​29133+1162+3​29133+1=3.434841368⋯x_{3}=\frac{1}{3}\,\sqrt[3]{162+3\,\sqrt{2913}}+{\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{162+3\,\sqrt{2913}}}}+1=3.434841368\cdots. It follows that

x2=3.701562118≱4=⌈3.434841368⋯⌉=⌈x3⌉.x_{2}=3.701562118\not\geq 4=\lceil 3.434841368\cdots\rceil=\lceil x_{3}\rceil.

On the other hand (1,4,5,2)(1,4,5,2) is the ff-vector of the simplicial complex given by two triangles glued along an edge.

Remark 3.0.

Note that the assumption xi−1≥⌈xi⌉x_{i-1}\geq\lceil x_{i}\rceil of Theorem 3.0 is sometimes satisfied by ff-polynomials of simplicial complexes having imaginary roots. For example, f⁡(t)=1+4​t+6​t2+3​t3=1+(41)​t+(42)​t2+(3.747836837⋯3)​t3f(t)=1+4t+6t^{2}+3t^{3}=1+\binom{4}{1}t+\binom{4}{2}t^{2}+\binom{3.747836837\cdots}{3}t^{3} is not real-rooted. It is the ff-polynomial of the boundary of the tetrahedron with the interior of one triangle removed. On the other hand xi−1≥⌈xi⌉x_{i-1}\geq\lceil x_{i}\rceil is still satisfied.

Remark 3.0.

The following example shows that if the binomial expansion (x1,…,xd)(x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}) of the ff-vector of a simplicial complex satisfies xi−1≥⌈xi⌉x_{i-1}\geq\lceil x_{i}\rceil for i=2,…,di=2,\ldots,d then the corresponding ff-polynomial f⁡(t)f(t) is not necessarily real-rooted, indeed not even log-concave. The polynomial f⁡(t)=1+10​t+3​t2+t3=1+(101)​t+(32)​t2+(33)​t3f(t)=1+10t+3t^{2}+t^{3}=1+\binom{10}{1}t+\binom{3}{2}t^{2}+\binom{3}{3}t^{3} is the ff-polynomial of a triangle together with 77 isolated vertices. Clearly, 10≥3≥310\geq 3\geq 3 but 9=32≱1⋅10=109=3^{2}\not\geq 1\cdot 10=10.

3.2. Second approach

We further advance our understanding of Question 1.0 by conjecturing a stronger result which implies an affirmative answer to the question. Let f⁡(t)=1+f0​t+⋯+fd−1​td∈ℕ⁡[t]f(t)=1+f_{0}t+\cdots+f_{d-1}t^{d}\in\mathbb{N}[t] and let f⁡(t)=1+(x11)​t+⋯+(xdd)​td∈ℕ⁡[t]f(t)=1+\binom{x_{1}}{1}t+\cdots+\binom{x_{d}}{d}t^{d}\in\mathbb{N}[t] be its binomial expansion. Further let

fi−1=(aii)+(ai−1i−1)+⋯+(ajj), for ​ai>⋯>aj≥j≥1f_{i-1}=\binom{a_{i}}{i}+\binom{a_{i-1}}{i-1}+\cdots+\binom{a_{j}}{j},\text{ for }a_{i}>\cdots>a_{j}\geq j\geq 1

be the iith binomial expansion of fi−1f_{i-1}. For i≥1i\geq 1, we define gig_{i} and hi−1h_{i-1} by

gi=(ai−1i)+(ai−1−1i−1)+⋯+(aj−1j)g_{i}=\binom{a_{i}-1}{i}+\binom{a_{i-1}-1}{i-1}+\cdots+\binom{a_{j}-1}{j}

and

hi−1=(ai−1i−1)+(ai−1−1i−2)+⋯+(aj−1j−1).h_{i-1}=\binom{a_{i}-1}{i-1}+\binom{a_{i-1}-1}{i-2}+\cdots+\binom{a_{j}-1}{j-1}.

It is easily seen that h0=1h_{0}=1 and fi−1=gi+hi−1f_{i-1}=g_{i}+h_{i-1}. In particular, we have

f⁡(t)=1+∑i=1dfi−1​ti=( 1+∑i=1dgi​ti)+t⁡( 1+∑i=2dhi−1​ti−1).f(t)=1+\sum_{i=1}^{d}f_{i-1}t^{i}=\Big(\,1+\sum_{i=1}^{d}g_{i}t^{i}\,\Big)+t\Big(\,1+\sum_{i=2}^{d}h_{i-1}t^{i-1}\,\Big).

We call the decomposition f⁡(t)=g⁡(t)+t​h​(t)f(t)=g(t)+th(t) with g⁡(t)=1+∑i=1dgi​tig(t)=1+\sum_{i=1}^{d}g_{i}t^{i} and h⁡(t)=1+∑i=1d−1hi​tih(t)=1+\sum_{i=1}^{d-1}h_{i}t^{i} the recursive decomposition of f⁡(t)f(t).

We will show that a positive answer to the following conjecture implies a positive answer to Question 1.0.

Conjecture 3.0.

Let f⁡(t)=1+f0​t+⋯+fd−1​td∈ℕ⁡[t]f(t)=1+f_{0}t+\cdots+f_{d-1}t^{d}\in\mathbb{N}[t] have only real roots and recursive decomposition f⁡(t)=g⁡(t)+t​h​(t)f(t)=g(t)+th(t), with

g⁡(t)=1+g1​t+⋯+gd​td,h⁡(t)=1+h1​t+⋯+hd−1​td−1.g(t)=1+g_{1}t+\cdots+g_{d}t^{d},\ \ h(t)=1+h_{1}t+\cdots+h_{d-1}t^{d-1}.

Then for i=1,…,d−1i=1,\dots,d-1, we have hi≤gih_{i}\leq g_{i}.

Proposition 3.0.

If Conjecture 3.0 holds then Question 1.0 has a positive answer.

Proof.

Let

fi−1=(aii)+(ai−1i−1)+⋯+(ajj), for ai>⋯aj≥j≥1,f_{i-1}=\binom{a_{i}}{i}+\binom{a_{i-1}}{i-1}+\cdots+\binom{a_{j}}{j},\text{ for }a_{i}>\cdots a_{j}\geq j\geq 1,

and

fi=(bi+1i+1)+(bii)+⋯+(brr), for ​bi+1>⋯>br≥r≥1f_{i}=\binom{b_{i+1}}{i+1}+\binom{b_{i}}{i}+\cdots+\binom{b_{r}}{r},\text{ for }b_{i+1}>\cdots>b_{r}\geq r\geq 1

be the iith binomial expansion of fi−1f_{i-1} and the (i+1)(i+1)st binomial expansion of fif_{i}. Then

gi=(ai−1i)+(ai−1−1i−1)+⋯+(aj−1j)g_{i}=\binom{a_{i}-1}{i}+\binom{a_{i-1}-1}{i-1}+\cdots+\binom{a_{j}-1}{j}

and

hi=(bi+1−1i)+(bi−1i)+⋯+(br−1r−1).h_{i}=\binom{b_{i+1}-1}{i}+\binom{b_{i}-1}{i}+\cdots+\binom{b_{r}-1}{r-1}.

After canceling identical terms in the binomial expansions and using (1) it follows that hi≤gih_{i}\leq g_{i} if and only if (bi+1,bi,…,br)≤l​e​x(ai,ai−1,…,aj)(b_{i+1},b_{i},\dots,b_{r})\leq_{lex}(a_{i},a_{i-1},\dots,a_{j}) in the lexicographic order. Note that

μi+1​(fi)=(bi+1i)+(bii−1)+⋯+(brr−1).\mu_{i+1}(f_{i})=\binom{b_{i+1}}{i}+\binom{b_{i}}{i-1}+\cdots+\binom{b_{r}}{r-1}.

If (bi+1,bi,…,br)≤l​e​x(ai,ai−1,…,aj)(b_{i+1},b_{i},\dots,b_{r})\leq_{lex}(a_{i},a_{i-1},\dots,a_{j}) then we have μi+1​(fi)≤fi−1\mu_{i+1}(f_{i})\leq f_{i-1}. The assertion now follows.

∎

Some calculations on the Eulerian polynomial and the Stirling polynomial of the second kind suggest a positive answer, upon which we pose the following question.

Question 3.0.

Let f⁡(t)=1+f0​t+⋯+fd−1​td∈ℕ⁡[t]f(t)=1+f_{0}t+\cdots+f_{d-1}t^{d}\in\mathbb{N}[t] be a polynomial with only real roots and let f⁡(t)=g⁡(t)+t​h​(t)f(t)=g(t)+th(t) its recursive decomposition. Is true that g⁡(t)g(t) and h⁡(t)h(t) both have only real roots?

After this paper was published, in a parallel development, Anish Patil and the authors found examples showing that the answer to the question is negative in general. The example provided to us by Anish Patil is particularly simple. Let f⁡(t)=(1+3​t)3f(t)=(1+3t)^{3} then the recursive decomposition is given by g⁡(t)=(1+t)​(1+7​t+13​t2)g(t)=(1+t)(1+7t+13t^{2}) and h⁡(t)=1+7​t+14​t2h(t)=1+7t+14t^{2}. While f⁡(t)f(t) clearly has only real roots, the quadratic polynomials 1+7​t+13​t21+7t+13t^{2} and 1+7​t+14​t21+7t+14t^{2} have no real roots. After being informed by Anish Patil about this counterexample the paper Feihu Liu, Ying Wang, Zihao Zhang posted a paper [14] with results and counterexamples completely clarifying the boundaries between yes and no answers to the question.

3.3. Third approach

To affirmatively answer another special case of Question 1.0, we consider certain vectors studied by Murai [16]. Let f=(1,f0,…,fd−1)∈ℤd+1f=(1,f_{0},\dots,f_{d-1})\in\mathbb{Z}^{d+1} be the ff-vector of a simplicial complex. We say that a vector α=(0,1,α0,…,αd−2)∈ℤd+1\alpha=(0,1,\alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{d-2})\in\mathbb{Z}^{d+1} is a basic admissible vector of ff if

  • (BA1)

    (1,α0,…,αd−2)∈ℤd(1,\alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{d-2})\in\mathbb{Z}^{d} is the ff-vector of a simplicial complex;

  • (BA2)

    fi≥αif_{i}\geq\alpha_{i} for i=0,1,…,d−2i=0,1,\dots,d-2.

A vector β∈ℤd+1\beta\in\mathbb{Z}^{d+1} is admissible to ff if there exists a sequence of vectors β1,…,βt∈ℤd+1\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{t}\in\mathbb{Z}^{d+1} such that

  • (A1)

    β=β1+⋯+βt\beta=\beta_{1}+\cdots+\beta_{t};

  • (A2)

    βi\beta_{i} is a basic admissible vector of f+β1+⋯+βi−1f+\beta_{1}+\cdots+\beta_{i-1} for i=1,2,…,ti=1,2,\dots,t.

Lemma 3.1 (Lemma 3.1 (1)(3)[16]).

Let f=(1,f0,…,fd−1)∈ℤd+1f=(1,f_{0},\dots,f_{d-1})\in\mathbb{Z}^{d+1} be the ff-vector of a simplicial complex and let α=(0,1,α0,…,αd−2),β=(0,1,β0,…,βd−2)∈ℤd+1\alpha=(0,1,\alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{d-2}),\beta=(0,1,\beta_{0},\ldots,\beta_{d-2})\in\mathbb{Z}^{d+1} be admissible to ff. Then

  • (i)

    f+αf+\alpha is the ff-vector of a simplicial complex.

  • (ii)

    α+β\alpha+\beta is admissible to ff.

The next proposition will be key to the proof that some real-rooted classical polynomials are ff-polynomials.

Proposition 3.0.

Let f⁡(t)f(t) be an ff-polynomial of a simplicial complex. Then f⁡(t)+t​f′​(t)f(t)+tf^{\prime}(t) is an ff-polynomial of a simplicial complex.

Proof.

Suppose that f⁡(t)=1+f0​t+⋯+fd−1​tdf(t)=1+f_{0}t+\cdots+f_{d-1}t^{d} is an ff-polynomial of a simplicial complex Δ\Delta. Then f=(1,f0,…,fd−1)∈ℤd+1f=(1,f_{0},\dots,f_{d-1})\in\mathbb{Z}^{d+1} is the ff-vector of Δ\Delta. Let β=(0,f0,2​f1,…,d​fd−1)∈ℤd+1\beta=(0,f_{0},2f_{1},\dots,df_{d-1})\in\mathbb{Z}^{d+1}. Then by Lemma 3.1, to show that f⁡(t)+t​f′​(t)f(t)+tf^{\prime}(t) is an ff-polynomial of a simplicial complex it suffices to show β\beta is an admissible vector of ff. For each vertex viv_{i}, i=1,…,f0i=1,\ldots,f_{0}, of Δ\Delta let βi=(0,1,β0(i),…,βd−2(i))\beta_{i}=(0,1,\beta_{0}^{(i)},\ldots,\beta_{d-2}^{(i)}), where (1,β0(i),…,βd−2(i))(1,\beta_{0}^{(i)},\ldots,\beta_{d-2}^{(i)}) is the ff-vector of the link of viv_{i} in Δ\Delta. Then (BA1) is satisfied for all βi\beta_{i} by definition. Since the (i−1)(i-1)-faces of the link of a vertex are in one to one correspondence with a subset of the ii-faces of Δ\Delta, condition (BA2) follows for all βi\beta_{i}. Indeed it follows for all βi\beta_{i} and for any complex having an ff-vector which is coordinatewise greater or equal to (1,f0,…,fd−1)(1,f_{0},\dots,f_{d-1}). Using this and Lemma 3.1(i),(ii) inductively it then follows that f+β1+⋯+βi−1f+\beta_{1}+\cdots+\beta_{i-1} is a basic admissible vector of f+β1+⋯+βif+\beta_{1}+\cdots+\beta_{i} for i=1,…,f0i=1,\ldots,f_{0}. In particular, Lemma 3.1 implies that f+βf+\beta is an ff-vector.

Since a single ii-face of Δ\Delta gives rise to exactly i+1i+1 faces of dimension i−1i-1 in the links of its vertices it follows that β=(0,f0,2​f1,…,d​fd−1)\beta=(0,f_{0},2f_{1},\ldots,df_{d-1}) and the assertion follows. ∎

The following corollary will turn out to be very useful when analyzing sequences defined through recursions.

Corollary 3.0.

Let (1,f0,…,fd−1)(1,f_{0},\dots,f_{d-1}) be the ff-vector of a simplicial complex. Then

μi+1​((i+2)​fi)≤(i+1)​fi−1​ for ​1≤i≤d−1.\mu_{i+1}\big(\,(i+2)f_{i}\,\big)\leq(i+1)\,f_{i-1}\text{ for }1\leq i\leq d-1.
Proof.

Basic calculus shows that for f⁡(t)=1+∑i=1dfi−1​tif(t)=1+\sum_{i=1}^{d}f_{i-1}t^{i} we have that f⁡(t)+t​f′​(t)=1+2​f0​t+⋯+(d+1)​fd−1f(t)+tf^{\prime}(t)=1+2f_{0}t+\cdots+(d+1)f_{d-1}. By Proposition 3.0 it follows that (1,2​f0,3​f1,…,(i+2)​fi,…,(d+1)​fd−1)(1,2f_{0},3f_{1},\dots,(i+2)f_{i},\dots,(d+1)f_{d-1}) is the ff-vector of a simplicial complex. Then by Theorem 2.0, the result follows. ∎

We now want to apply these results to show that Eulerian, Stirling and derangement polynomials are ff-polynomials. Instead of giving three separate proofs, we consider arrays [Td,k]d,k∈ℤ\big[\,T_{d,k}\,\big]_{d,k\in\mathbb{Z}} of integers which satisfy the following conditions:

  • (R1)

    T1,0=1T_{1,0}=1,

  • (R2)

    Td,k=0T_{d,k}=0 for all dd and kk which do not satisfy 0≤k≤d−10\leq k\leq d-1,

  • (R3)

    For i=1,2,3i=1,2,3 there are integers r(i),s(i),t(i)r^{(i)},s^{(i)},t^{(i)} such that

    • (i)

      r(1)=0r^{(1)}=0 and t(1)=1t^{(1)}=1,

    • (ii)

      s(i)≤t(i)s^{(i)}\leq t^{(i)},

    • (iii)

      for all 0≤k≤d−10\leq k\leq d-1 and d≥2d\geq 2 we have ad,k(i):=r(i)​d+s(i)​k+t(i)≥0a_{d,k}^{(i)}:=r^{(i)}d+s^{(i)}k+t^{(i)}\geq 0.

  • (R4)

    For 0≤k≤d−10\leq k\leq d-1 and d≥2d\geq 2 we have

    Td,k=ad,k(1)​Td−1,k+ad,k(2)​Td−1,k−1+ad,k(3)​Td−2,k−1.\displaystyle T_{d,k}=a_{d,k}^{(1)}T_{d-1,k}+a_{d,k}^{(2)}T_{d-1,k-1}+a_{d,k}^{(3)}T_{d-2,k-1}.

For the following choices of parameters we recover Eulerian, Stirling and derangement numbers and verify that (R1)-(R4) are satisfied.

  • •

    (Eulerian) [Td,k]d≥1,k≥0[T_{d,k}]_{d\geq 1,k\geq 0} is the Eulerian triangle, with Td,kT_{d,k} the number of permutations in SdS_{d} with kk descents (see [17, A008292]) for ad,k(1)=k+1=0⋅d+1⋅k+1a_{d,k}^{(1)}=k+1=0\cdot d+1\cdot k+1, ad,k(2)=d−k=1⋅d+(−1)⋅k+0a_{d,k}^{(2)}=d-k=1\cdot d+(-1)\cdot k+0 and ad,k(3)=0=0⋅d+0⋅k+0a_{d,k}^{(3)}=0=0\cdot d+0\cdot k+0.

  • •

    (Stirling) [Td,k]d≥1,k≥0[T_{d,k}]_{d\geq 1,k\geq 0} is the Stirling triangle of the second kind, with T⁡(d,k)T(d,k) the number of set partitions of {1,…,d}\{1,\ldots,d\} with k+1k+1 blocks (see [17, A008277]) for ad,k(1)=k+1=0⋅d+1⋅k+1a_{d,k}^{(1)}=k+1=0\cdot d+1\cdot k+1, ad,k(2)=1=0⋅d+0⋅k+1a_{d,k}^{(2)}=1=0\cdot d+0\cdot k+1 and ad,k(3)=0=0⋅d+0⋅k+0a_{d,k}^{(3)}=0=0\cdot d+0\cdot k+0.

  • •

    (Derangements) Td,kT_{d,k} is the number of derangements of [d][d] having kk exceedances (see [17, A046739]) for ad,k(1)=k+1=0⋅d+1⋅k+1a_{d,k}^{(1)}=k+1=0\cdot d+1\cdot k+1, ad,k(2)=d−k=1⋅d+(−1)⋅k+0a_{d,k}^{(2)}=d-k=1\cdot d+(-1)\cdot k+0 and ad,k(3)=1⋅d+0⋅k+0a_{d,k}^{(3)}=1\cdot d+0\cdot k+0.

Theorem 3.0.

Let [Td,k]d,k∈ℤ[T_{d,k}]_{d,k\in\mathbb{Z}} be a triangular array defined satisfying (R1), (R2), (R3) and (R4). Then the ddth row polynomial Td​(t)=∑k≥0Td,k​tkT_{d}(t)=\displaystyle{\sum_{k\geq 0}}T_{d,k}t^{k} is an ff-polynomial of a simplicial complex.

Proof.

Note that by (R2) and (R4) Td,0=ad,0(1)​Td−1,0T_{d,0}=a_{d,0}^{(1)}T_{d-1,0} for d≥2d\geq 2. Now (R1) and (R3)(i) imply Td,0=1T_{d,0}=1 for all d≥1d\geq 1.

We prove the assertion by induction on dd.

For d=1d=1 condition (R1) and (R2) imply that T1​(t)=1T_{1}(t)=1 is the ff-polynomial of the simplicial complex {∅}\{\emptyset\}.

For d=2d=2 we have by (R1), (R2) and (R3)(iii) that T2,1=a2,1(2)≥0T_{2,1}=a_{2,1}^{(2)}\geq 0. Furthermore, (1,a2,1(2))(1,a_{2,1}^{(2)}) is the ff-polynomial of the simplicial complex consisting of a2,1(2)a_{2,1}^{(2)} simplices of dimension 00 and the empty set.

Suppose that d≥3d\geq 3 and for n≤d−1n\leq d-1 all Tn​(t)T_{n}(t) are ff-polynomials of simplicial complexes. By Theorem 2.0 we need to show that for 1≤k≤d−11\leq k\leq d-1 we have μk​(Td,k)≤Td,k−1\mu_{k}(T_{d,k})\leq T_{d,k-1}.

We will repeatedly use the fact that μk\mu_{k} is a subadditive function on non-negative integers (i.e., μk​(a+b)≤μk​(a)+μk​(b)\mu_{k}(a+b)\leq\mu_{k}(a)+\mu_{k}(b)). For that we first extend μk\mu_{k} to all non-negative integers by setting μk​(0)=0\mu_{k}(0)=0. It is easily checked that the subadditivity of μk\mu_{k} on positive integers (see [1, Theorem 7.4.2] or [6]) extends. We mark arguments using the subadditivity by (s​u​b)(sub).

Claim: For d≥3d\geq 3 and 0≤k≤d−10\leq k\leq d-1 we have

  • (1)

    μk​(ad,k(1)​Td−1,k)≤ad,k−1(1)​Td−1,k−1\mu_{k}\left(a_{d,k}^{(1)}T_{d-1,k}\right)\leq a_{d,k-1}^{(1)}T_{d-1,k-1},

  • (2)

    μk​(ad,k(2)​Td−1,k−1)≤ad,k−1(2)​Td−1,k−2\mu_{k}\left(a_{d,k}^{(2)}T_{d-1,k-1}\right)\leq a_{d,k-1}^{(2)}T_{d-1,k-2},

  • (3)

    μk​(ad,k(3)​Td−2,k−1)≤ad,k−1(3)​Td−2,k−2\mu_{k}\left(a_{d,k}^{(3)}T_{d-2,k-1}\right)\leq a_{d,k-1}^{(3)}T_{d-2,k-2}.

We prove the inequality (1) of the claim. The others then follow by similar reasoning.

Case: s(1)≤0s^{(1)}\leq 0.

By the induction hypothesis for d−1d-1 and since by (R3)(iii) ad,k(1)≥0a_{d,k}^{(1)}\geq 0, we have

μk​(ad,k(1)​Td−1,k)\displaystyle\mu_{k}\left(a_{d,k}^{(1)}T_{d-1,k}\right) =(R3)​μk​((r(1)​d+s(1)​k+t(1))​Td−1,k)\displaystyle\overset{\text{(R3)}}{=}\mu_{k}\left((r^{(1)}d+s^{(1)}k+t^{(1)})\,T_{d-1,k}\right)
≤(s​u​b)​(r(1)​d+t(1))​μk​(Td−1,k)+s(1)​μk​(k​Td−1,k)\displaystyle\overset{(sub)}{\leq}(r^{(1)}d+t^{(1)})\,\mu_{k}(T_{d-1,k})+s^{(1)}\mu_{k}(kT_{d-1,k})
≤Corollary 3.0​(r(1)​d+t(1))​μk​(Td−1,k)+s(1)​(k−1)​Td−1,k−1\displaystyle\overset{\text{\ref{f-vector}}}{\leq}(r^{(1)}d+t^{(1)})\,\mu_{k}(T_{d-1,k})+s^{(1)}(k-1)\,T_{d-1,k-1}
≤Induction​(r(1)​d+s(1)​(k−1)+t(1))​Td−1,k−1\displaystyle\overset{\text{Induction}}{\leq}(r^{(1)}d+s^{(1)}(k-1)+t^{(1)})\,T_{d-1,k-1}
=(R3)​ad,k−1(1)​Td−1,k−1.\displaystyle\overset{\text{(R3)}}{=}a_{d,k-1}^{(1)}T_{d-1,k-1}.

Case: s(1)>0s^{(1)}>0.

By s(1)≤t(1)s^{(1)}\leq t^{(1)} and ad,k(1)≥0a_{d,k}^{(1)}\geq 0,

μk​(ad,k(1)​Td−1,k)\displaystyle\mu_{k}\left(a_{d,k}^{(1)}\,T_{d-1,k}\right) =(R3)​μk​((r(1)​d+s(1)​k+t(1))​Td−1,k)\displaystyle\overset{\text{(R3)}}{=}\mu_{k}\left((r^{(1)}d+s^{(1)}k+t^{(1)})\,T_{d-1,k}\right)
=μk​((r(1)​d+s(1)​(k+1)+t(1)−s(1))​Td−1,k)\displaystyle=\mu_{k}\left((r^{(1)}d+s^{(1)}(k+1)+t^{(1)}-s^{(1)})\,T_{d-1,k}\right)
≤(s​u​b)​μk​(s(1)​(k+1)​Td−1,k)+μk​((r(1)​d+t(1)−s(1))​Td−1,k)\displaystyle\overset{(sub)}{\leq}\mu_{k}\left(s^{(1)}(k+1)\,T_{d-1,k}\right)+\mu_{k}\left((r^{(1)}d+t^{(1)}-s^{(1)})\,T_{d-1,k}\right)
≤Corollary 3.0​s(1)​k​Td−1,k−1+μk​((r(1)​d+t(1)−s(1))​Td−1,k)\displaystyle\overset{\text{\ref{f-vector}}}{\leq}s^{(1)}k\,T_{d-1,k-1}+\mu_{k}\left((r^{(1)}d+t^{(1)}-s^{(1)})\,T_{d-1,k}\right)
≤Induction​(r(1)​d+s(1)​k+t(1)−s(1))​Td−1,k−1\displaystyle\overset{\text{Induction}}{\leq}(r^{(1)}d+s^{(1)}k+t^{(1)}-s^{(1)})\,T_{d-1,k-1}
=(R​3)​ad,k−1(1)​Td−1,k−1,\displaystyle\overset{(R3)}{=}a_{d,k-1}^{(1)}T_{d-1,k-1},

This completes the proof of the claim. Using (R4) and (R3)(iii) we conclude

μk​(Td,k)\displaystyle\mu_{k}(T_{d,k}) =(R4)​μk​(ad,k(1)​Td−1,k+ad,k(2)​Td−1,k−1+ad,k(3)​Td−2,k−1)\displaystyle\overset{\text{(R4)}}{=}\mu_{k}\left(a_{d,k}^{(1)}T_{d-1,k}+a_{d,k}^{(2)}T_{d-1,k-1}+a_{d,k}^{(3)}T_{d-2,k-1}\right)
≤(s​u​b)​μk​(ad,k(1)​Td−1,k)+μk​(ad,k(2)​Td−1,k−1)+μk​(ad,k(3)​Td−2,k−1)\displaystyle\overset{(sub)}{\leq}\mu_{k}\left(a_{d,k}^{(1)}T_{d-1,k}\right)+\mu_{k}\left(a_{d,k}^{(2)}T_{d-1,k-1}\right)+\mu_{k}\left(a_{d,k}^{(3)}T_{d-2,k-1}\right)
≤(Claim)​ad,k−1(1)​Td−1,k−1+ad,k−1(2)​Td−1,k−2+ad,k−1(3)​Td−2,k−2\displaystyle\overset{\text{(Claim)}}{\leq}a_{d,k-1}^{(1)}T_{d-1,k-1}+a_{d,k-1}^{(2)}T_{d-1,k-2}+a_{d,k-1}^{(3)}T_{d-2,k-2}
=(R4)​Td,k−1.\displaystyle\overset{\text{(R4)}}{=}T_{d,k-1}.

The assertion now follows. ∎

Since we have already verified conditions (R1)-(R4) for these classical polynomials the following corollary is an immediate consequence of Theorem 3.0. The case of the Eulerian polynomial is known by work of Edelman and Reiner [7] and Gasharov [10]. For the other two we are not aware of any reference.

Corollary 3.0.

The Eulerian polynomial, the Stirling polynomial of the second kind and the derangement polynomial are ff-polynomials of simplicial complexes.

4. Preserving real-rootedness preserves the f−f-vector property

In this section we collect results which show that well studied constructions on polynomials, that preserve real-rootedness, also preserve the property of being the ff-polynomial of a simplicial complex. Since for a real-rooted polynomial f⁡(t)f(t) the polynomial f​(t)+f′​(t)​tf(t)+f^{\prime}(t)\,t is also real-rooted, Proposition 3.0 is another result in this direction.

We start with the dilation of the variable. Elementary analysis shows that if f⁡(t)f(t) is a polynomial with only real roots then same holds for f⁡(c​t)f(ct) for any c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}.

Proposition 4.0.

Let f⁡(t)f(t) be an ff-polynomial of a simplicial complex. Then for any positive c∈ℤc\in\mathbb{Z} the polynomial f⁡(c​t)f(ct) is an ff-polynomial of a simplicial complex.

Proof.

Let Δ\Delta be a simplicial complex on vertex set [d][d]. We construct a simplicial complex Δc\Delta^{c} on vertex set [d]×[c][d]\times[c]. Define π\pi: [d]×[c]→[d][d]\times[c]\rightarrow[d] by π⁡((,,,))=i\pi\big(\,(i,j)\,\big)=i. For σ⊆[d]×[c]\sigma\subseteq[d]\times[c] we set σ∈Δc\sigma\in\Delta^{c} if and only if π⁡(σ)∈Δ\pi(\sigma)\in\Delta. Thus for any ii-simplex σ∈Δ\sigma\in\Delta there are ci+1c^{i+1} simplices of dimension ii in Δc\Delta^{c}. It follows that if f⁡(x)f(x) is the ff-polynomial of Δ\Delta then f⁡(c​x)f(cx) is the ff-polynomial of Δc\Delta^{c}. ∎

It is easily seen that if (an)n≥0(a_{n})_{n\geq 0} is a Pólya-frequency sequence, then so is (ak​n)n≥0(a_{kn})_{n\geq 0} for any natural number k≥1k\geq 1 (see e.g. [5]). In particular by the Aissen-Edrei-Schoenberg-Whitney Theorem, if f⁡(t)=1+f0​t+⋯+fd−1​tdf(t)=1+f_{0}t+\cdots+f_{d-1}t^{d} is real-rooted then so is 1+fk−1​t+f2​k−1​t2+⋯1+f_{k-1}t+f_{2k-1}t^{2}+\cdots. For proving the following result we will resort to methods from combinatorial commutative algebra and the theory of Gröbner bases. In the proof we will use these methods freely and refer the reader to [11] for further details.

Proposition 4.0.

Let f=(1,f0,…,fd−1)f=(1,f_{0},\ldots,f_{d-1}) be the ff-vector of a simplicial complex. Then for any k≥1k\geq 1 the vector (1,fk−1,f2​k−1,…)(1,f_{k-1},f_{2k-1},\ldots) is the ff-vector of a simplicial complex.

Proof.

For this result we use the fact that (1,f0,…,fd−1)(1,f_{0},\ldots,f_{d-1}) is the ff-vector of a simplicial complex if and only if for any field 𝕂\mathbb{K} there is a number nn and a squarefree monomial ideal II in S=𝕂⁡[x1,…,xn]S=\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] such that the Hilbert series of R=S/(I+(x12,…,xn2))R=S/\big(\,I+(x_{1}^{2},\ldots,x_{n}^{2})\,\big) is 1+f0​t+⋯+fd−1​td1+f_{0}t+\cdots+f_{d-1}t^{d}. In the latter case we have a direct sum decomposition as 𝕂\mathbb{K}-vector spaces R=A0⊕A1⊕⋯⊕Ad−1R=A_{0}\oplus A_{1}\oplus\cdots\oplus A_{d-1} where AiA_{i} is the subspace generated by the cosets of the homogeneous polynomials of degree ii and is of 𝕂\mathbb{K}-dimension fi−1f_{i-1}. Now R⟨k⟩=A0⊕Ak⊕A2​k⊕⋯R^{\langle k\rangle}=A_{0}\oplus A_{k}\oplus A_{2k}\oplus\cdots is known as the kkth Veronese algebra of AA. We can write R⟨k⟩R^{\langle k\rangle} as the image of

T=𝕂⁡[yℓ1,…,ℓn|ℓ1+⋯+ℓn=k​ and ​ℓi≥1]T=\mathbb{K}\big[\,y_{\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{n}}~\big|~\ell_{1}+\cdots+\ell_{n}=k\text{ and }\ell_{i}\geq 1\,\big]

by the homomorphism ϕ\phi which sends yℓ1,…,ℓny_{\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{n}} to x1ℓ1⋯xnℓnx_{1}^{\ell_{1}}\cdots x_{n}^{\ell_{n}}. Since xi2=0x_{i}^{2}=0 in RR it follows that all yℓ1,…,ℓn2y_{\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{n}}^{2} lie in the kernel of ϕ\phi. Let MM be the ideal generated by the yℓ1,…,ℓn2y_{\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{n}}^{2} and JJ be such that J+M=ker⁡(ϕ)J+M=\ker(\phi). Let ⪯\preceq be a term order. Then T/(M+J)T/(M+J) and T/i​n⪯​(M+J)T/{\mathrm{i}n}_{\preceq}{(M+J)} share the same Hilbert series, where i​n⪯​(M+J){\mathrm{i}n}_{\preceq}(M+J) denotes the initial ideal of M+JM+J. Since MM is a monomial ideal we clearly have M⊆i​n⪯​(M+J)M\subseteq{\mathrm{i}n}_{\preceq}(M+J). Since i​n⪯​(M+J){\mathrm{i}n}_{\preceq}(M+J) also is a monomial ideal it follows that i​n⪯​(J+M)=J′+M{\mathrm{i}n}_{\preceq}(J+M)=J^{\prime}+M for a squarefree monomial ideal J′J^{\prime}. From this we deduce that (1,fk−1,f2​k−1,…)(1,f_{k-1},f_{2k-1},\ldots) is an ff-vector. ∎

The fact that products of real-rooted polynomials are real-rooted is trivial. Also the first part of the following proposition, which is the ff-vector analog of this statement is well known. The real-rootedness of the Hadamard product of two real-rooted polynomials is again a known fact (see e.g. [9]).

Proposition 4.0.

Let f⁡(t)=1+f0​t+⋯+fd−1​tdf(t)=1+f_{0}t+\cdots+f_{d-1}t^{d} and g⁡(t)=1+g0​t+⋯+gd′−1​td′g(t)=1+g_{0}t+\cdots+g_{d^{\prime}-1}t^{d^{\prime}} be two ff-polynomials of simplicial complexes. Then the product f⁡(t)​g​(t)f(t)g(t) and the Hadamard product f⁡(t)∘g⁡(t)=1+f0​g0​t+f1​g1​t2+⋯+fmin⁡{d,d′}​gmin⁡{d,d′}​tmin⁡{d,d′}+1f(t)\circ g(t)=1+f_{0}g_{0}\,t+f_{1}g_{1}\,t^{2}+\cdots+f_{\min\{d,d^{\prime}\}}g_{\min\{d,d^{\prime}\}}\,t^{\min\{d,d^{\prime}\}+1} are ff-polynomials of simplicial complexes.

Proof.

Let Δ\Delta be a simplicial complex over ground set Ω\Omega with ff-vector (1,f0,…,fd−1)(1,f_{0},\ldots,f_{d-1}) and let Δ′\Delta^{\prime} be a simplicial complex over ground set Ω′\Omega^{\prime} with ff-vector (1,g0,…,gd′−1)(1,g_{0},\ldots,g_{d^{\prime}-1}). We can assume that Ω\Omega and Ω′\Omega^{\prime} are disjoint.

Ordinary Product: The join Δ∗Δ′\Delta*\Delta^{\prime} of Δ\Delta and Δ′\Delta^{\prime} is defined as the simplicial complex whose ii-dimensional simplices are unions σ∪τ\sigma\cup\tau for a jj-dimensional simplex σ∈Δ\sigma\in\Delta and (i−j−1)(i-j-1)-dimensional simplex τ\tau of Δ′\Delta^{\prime} for some −1≤j≤i-1\leq j\leq i. By disjointness of Ω\Omega and Ω′\Omega^{\prime} it follows that the number of ii-dimensional faces of Δ∗Δ′\Delta*\Delta^{\prime} is ∑j=−1ifj​gi−j−1\sum_{j=-1}^{i}f_{j}g_{i-j-1}. The latter expression is exactly the coefficient of tit^{i} in f⁡(t)​g​(t)f(t)g(t). In particular, f⁡(t)​g​(t)f(t)g(t) is the ff-polynomial of a simplicial complex.

Hadamard Product: We assume in addition that Ω\Omega and Ω′\Omega^{\prime} are linearly ordered by << and <′<^{\prime} respectively. Let Δ∘Δ′\Delta\circ\Delta^{\prime} be the simplicial complex over ground set Ω×Ω′\Omega\times\Omega^{\prime} where {(ω1,ω1′),…,(ωi,ωi′)}\{(\omega_{1},\omega_{1}^{\prime}),\ldots,(\omega_{i},\omega_{i}^{\prime})\} is a simplex in Δ⋅Δ′\Delta\cdot\Delta^{\prime} if any only if

  • •

    {ω1,…,ωi}∈Δ\{\omega_{1},\ldots,\omega_{i}\}\in\Delta and {ω1′,…,ωi′}∈Δ′\{\omega_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,\omega_{i}^{\prime}\}\in\Delta^{\prime} and

  • •

    ω1<⋯<ωi\omega_{1}<\cdots<\omega_{i} and ω1′<′⋯<′ωi′\omega_{1}^{\prime}<^{\prime}\cdots<^{\prime}\omega_{i}^{\prime}.

One easily checks that Δ∘Δ′\Delta\circ\Delta^{\prime} is a simplicial complex with ff-vector (f−1​g−1,f0​g0,⋯)(f_{-1}g_{-1},f_{0}g_{0},\cdots). ∎

As an example we apply the preceding proposition to Narayana polynomials of type B NnB​(t)=(n0)2+(n1)2​t+⋯+(nn)2​tnN_{n}^{B}(t)=\binom{n}{0}^{2}+\binom{n}{1}^{2}\,t+\cdots+\binom{n}{n}^{2}\,t^{n}. It is well known (see Example 5.8 in [8]) that NnB​(t)N_{n}^{B}(t) is the hh-polynomial of the simplicial complex dual to the associahedron of type BB – the cyclohedron. As a Hadamard product NnB​(t)=((1+t)n)∘((1+t)n)N_{n}^{B}(t)=\Big(\,(1+t)^{n}\,\Big)\circ\Big(\,(1+t)^{n}\,\Big) of a real-rooted polynomial with itself, NnB​(t)N_{n}^{B}(t) is real-rooted for any integer n≥1n\geq 1. Since (1+t)n(1+t)^{n} is the ff-polynomial of the simplex of dimension n−1n-1, the proposition implies that NnB​(t)N_{n}^{B}(t) is the ff-polynomial of a simplicial complex.
